newsitem.title: USA: Storm in Dakotas likely killed over 100,000 cattle.
newsitem.headline: Storm in Dakotas likely killed over 100,000 cattle.

text.p: Ranchers in North and South Dakota found grim reminders this week of an early April blizzard as snow began melting from more than 100,000 cattle and calves that died in blinding snow driven by 70-mph winds.

More losses are yet to come as stressed cows that survived may abort pregnancies or be unable to bear calves later, industry sources said. Also, surviving calves may later die of pneumonia or stress-related ailments.
"The saddest part is hearing of the illnesses," said Darlene Huettl, South Dakota Stock Growers Assn. spokesman.
South Dakota governmental agencies estimated 60,000 cattle and calves died in the storm, but Huettl said post-storm illnesses and abortions could quadruple that number.

The North Dakota Agricultural Statistics Service said losses in the southern half of that state may be unprecedented, with cattle and calf losses estimated at twice the normal death loss for this time of year.
The two states produce feeder cattle that primarily are sent to feedlots in Nebraska and the Midwest for fattening.
The U.S. Agriculture Department reported the two states had 5.7 million head as of January 1, or six percent of the total U.S. herd.
"We are finding more (dead cattle) every day as the snow melts," said Wade Moser, executive director of the North Dakota Stockmens' Association.
Moser estimated 100,000 calves died across the state, or about 10 percent of the calf crop. About 10,000 cows died but that toll may rise because "more cows were lost than we anticipated," he said.

Leet Fowler, a rancher in northwest South Dakota, lost about 75 calves and 150 cows in the April storm. Fence-high drifts had seven others walking off the ranch, and were later found alive 12 miles away.
"We had drifts that were over eight feet high. They just got buried," Fowler said of the cattle deaths.
Moser said the losses may financially wipe out some young ranchers and prompt others to retire.
Frigid cold and snow throughout the winter drained feed supplies and Moser said ranchers may run out of hay and other feed before spring pastures are ready for grazing.
"We are at least a month away from grass," he said. "I don't know what's going to happen. They cannot live on snowballs."
